title: Book 13
paragraphs: I call on you, O my God, my mercy, who created me and did not forget me even as I, forgetting you, was lost. I call you into my soul, which you are preparing for yourself by the longing you yourself inspire in it. Do not forsake me now as I call on you — you who went before me, calling out to me long before I called on you, and who pressed me with call after varied call, that I might hear you from far off, and turn, and call on you who had been calling after me. For you, Lord, blotted out all the evil I deserved, so as not to repay into my own hands what I had earned by falling away from you; and you went before all the good I might deserve, so as to repay instead the work of your own hands, by which you made me. For before I existed, you already were; and I was nothing that you could have granted to exist — and yet here I am, by your goodness alone, going ahead of all this that you have made me, and out of which you made me. For you had no need of me, nor am I any such good as to be of use to you, my Lord and God — not in serving you, as though you would tire from working, or as though your power might be diminished for lack of my service; nor in cultivating your service the way one cultivates land that would lie fallow unless I tended it — but in serving and worshiping you so that I might receive well-being from you, from whom comes the very fact that I have a being capable of well-being.

Your creature exists out of the fullness of your goodness — so that a good which could bring you no profit, and was not part of you (lest it be equal to you), might still exist, because it could be made by you. For what did heaven and earth, which you made in the beginning, deserve from you? Let those spiritual and bodily natures which you made in your wisdom say what they had done to deserve depending on you — even in that early, formless state of theirs, whether spiritual or bodily, on the verge of slipping away into a lawless freedom and a likeness to you grown very distant (the spiritual, though formless, ranking above the bodily even once formed, and the bodily, even formless, being better than nothing at all) — and so depending, formless as they were, on your Word, unless by that same Word they were brought back to your unity, given form, and made, from you the one sovereign good, altogether very good. How did they deserve from you even to exist without form, since they had not even been this except from you?

How did bodily matter deserve from you even to be invisible and formless? For it was not even this except that you made it — and so, because it did not exist, it could not have deserved to be made. Or how could that early, unformed spiritual creature deserve from you even to ebb and flow darkly like the deep — unlike you — unless it had been turned by that same Word to the one by whom it was created, and, enlightened by him, become light — not equally, yet in conformity with that Form which is equal to you? For just as in a body, to exist is not the same as to be beautiful, otherwise it could not be deformed; so likewise for a created spirit, to live is not the same as to live wisely, otherwise it would be wise unchangeably. But it is good for it always to hold fast to you, lest the light it has gained by turning to you it lose by turning away from you, and fall back into a life resembling the darksome deep. For we ourselves too, who as to the soul are a spiritual creature, turned away from you our light, and were once darkness in that life; and we still labor among the remnants of our darkness, until in your Only Son we become your righteousness, like the mountains of God. For we have been your judgments, which are like the great deep.

What you said at the beginning of creation — Let there be light, and there was light — I understand, not unfittingly, of the spiritual creature: because there already existed a kind of life that you might illuminate. But just as it had no claim on you for a life capable of being enlightened, so too, now that it existed, it had no claim to be enlightened. For its formless state could not please you unless it became light — and not merely by existing, but by beholding the illuminating light and clinging to it — so that its very living, and living happily, it owes to nothing but your grace, turned by a change for the better toward that which cannot be changed for worse or better: which you alone are, because you alone simply are; for you, to live and to live in blessedness are not two different things, since you are your own blessedness.

What then could be lacking to your good — which you yourself are — even if these things had never existed, or had remained formless? You made them not out of any need, but out of the fullness of your goodness, restraining them and turning them toward form, not as though your joy were completed by them. For to you, who are perfect, their imperfection is displeasing, and so they were perfected by you and please you — not as though you yourself were imperfect and were also to be perfected by their perfecting. For your good Spirit was indeed borne over the waters, not borne up by them, as if resting upon them. Those on whom your good Spirit is said to rest, he causes to rest in himself instead. But your incorruptible and unchangeable will, sufficient in itself for itself, was borne upon that life which you had created — for which living is not the same as living happily, since it lives also by ebbing and flowing in its own darkness — and which therefore remains to be turned to him by whom it was made, to live more and more by the fountain of life, to see light in his light, and to be perfected, enlightened, and made beautiful.

Now the Trinity appears to me, though in a glass darkly, and this is you, my God: because you, O Father, in him who is the Beginning of our wisdom, which is your Wisdom, born of yourself, equal to you and coeternal — that is, in your Son — created heaven and earth. We have already said much about the Heaven of heavens, and the earth invisible and without form, and the darksome deep, with reference to the wandering instability of its spiritual deformity, unless it had been turned to him from whom it had whatever degree of life it then had, and by his enlightening became a beautiful life, and the heaven of that heaven which was later set between water and water. And under the name of God I took the Father, who made these things; and under the name of Beginning, the Son, in whom he made these things; and believing, as I did, that my God is the Trinity, I searched further in his holy words, and behold, your Spirit moved upon the waters. There, my God, is the Trinity: Father, and Son, and Holy Ghost, Creator of all creation.

But what was the reason, O truthful Light? I lift my heart up to you — let it not teach me empty things, dispel its darkness — and tell me, I beg you, by our mother charity, tell me the reason, I beg you, why, after mentioning heaven, and the earth invisible and formless, and darkness over the deep, your Scripture should then finally mention your Spirit? It was because it was fitting that knowledge of him should be conveyed as being "borne above"; and this could not be said unless that over which your Spirit might be understood to have been borne had first been mentioned. For he was not borne above the Father, nor above the Son, nor could he rightly be said to be borne above if he were borne over nothing. So first had to be spoken of that over which he might be borne, and only then he, of whom it was fitting to speak in no other way than as being borne. But why was it not fitting that knowledge of him be conveyed in any way other than as being borne above?

So let anyone who can, follow with his understanding your Apostle, where he says: Because your love is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us; and where, concerning spiritual gifts, he teaches and shows us a more excellent way, the way of charity; and where he bends his knee to you on our behalf, that we may know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ. And so from the beginning he was borne, supreme, above the waters. To whom shall I say this? How can I speak of the weight of evil desires, dragging down toward the steep abyss, and how charity lifts us up again by your Spirit, who was borne above the waters? To whom shall I say it? How shall I say it? For it is not in space that we sink and rise. What could be more alike, and yet less alike? They are affections, they are loves — the uncleanness of our spirit flowing downward with the love of cares, and the holiness of yours lifting us upward with the love of untroubled rest — so that we may lift our hearts to you, where your Spirit is borne above the waters, and reach that supreme rest, when our soul shall have passed through the waters that give no support.

Angels fell away, man's soul fell away, and by falling they pointed to the abyss in that dark depth waiting for the whole spiritual creation, had you not said from the beginning, Let there be light, and there had been light, and every obedient intelligence of your heavenly city had clung to you and rested in your Spirit, which is borne unchangeably over everything changeable. Otherwise, even the heaven of heavens would in itself have been a darksome deep; but now it is light in the Lord. For even in that miserable restlessness of the spirits who fell away and discovered their own darkness, once stripped of the clothing of your light, you sufficiently reveal how noble you made the reasoning creature — for which nothing less than you will suffice to grant a happy rest, not even itself. For you, our God, will light up our darkness: from you comes our garment of light, and then our darkness will be as bright as noon. Give yourself to me, O my God, restore yourself to me: see, I love you, and if it is too little, I would love you more strongly. I cannot measure so as to know how much love I still lack, before my life may run into your embrace, and turn away no more, until it is hidden in the hidden place of your presence. This only I know: that woe is me, except in you — not only outside myself but within myself as well; and all abundance that is not my God is emptiness to me.

But was neither the Father nor the Son borne above the waters? If this means in space, as a body is, then neither was the Holy Spirit; but if it means the unchangeable supremacy of Divinity above all changeable things, then Father, Son, and Holy Spirit alike were borne upon the waters. Why then is this said only of your Spirit — why is it said of him alone? As if he had been in a place, he who is not in a place, of whom alone it is written that he is your gift? In your gift we rest; there we enjoy you. Our rest is our place. Love lifts us up there, and your good Spirit lifts up our lowliness from the gates of death. In your good pleasure is our peace. A body, by its own weight, strives toward its own place. Weight tends not only downward, but toward its own place. Fire rises, a stone falls; each is driven by its own weight, each seeks its own place. Oil poured under water rises above the water; water poured onto oil sinks below the oil; each is driven by its own weight to seek its own place. When things are out of their order they are restless; restored to order, they are at rest. My weight is my love; by it I am carried wherever I am carried. We are set aflame by your gift, and kindled, and carried upward; we glow within, and go forward. We climb the ascents that are in our heart, and sing a song of steps; we glow within with your fire, your good fire, and we go — because we go upward, toward the peace of Jerusalem. For I rejoiced when they said to me, We will go up to the house of the Lord. There your good pleasure has placed us, that we may desire nothing else but to dwell there forever.

Blessed creature, which, being itself other than you, has known no other condition than this: that as soon as it was made, it was — with no interval — by your gift, which is borne above everything changeable, lifted up by that calling in which you said, Let there be light, and there was light. Whereas in us this happened at different times, in that we were darkness and are made light; but of it is only said what it would have been, had it not been enlightened. And this is spoken as if it had been unsettled and dark beforehand, so that the cause by which it was made otherwise might appear — namely, that by turning to the unfailing Light it became light. Whoever can, let him understand this; let him ask it of you. Why should he trouble me, as if I could enlighten anyone who comes into this world?

Which of us comprehends the almighty Trinity? And yet which of us does not speak of it, if indeed it is it we speak of? Rare is the soul that, while speaking of it, knows what it is speaking of. And people argue and contend, yet without peace no one sees that vision. I wish that people would consider these three things that are within themselves. These three are indeed quite other than the Trinity — I only mean to point out where people can exercise themselves, and there test and feel how far short they fall. Now the three I meant are: to be, to know, and to will. For I am, and I know, and I will; I am knowing and willing; and I know myself to be, and to will; and I will to be, and to know. In these three, then, let whoever can discern how inseparable a life there is — indeed one life, one mind, one essence — and yet, finally, how inseparable a distinction there is, and yet a distinction. Surely a person has this before him; let him look into himself, and see, and tell me. But when he discovers and can say something about these, let him not therefore think he has found that which is above these — the Unchangeable, which is unchangeably, and knows unchangeably, and wills unchangeably; and whether, because of these three, there is also in God a Trinity, or whether all three are in each, so that the three belong to each, or whether both at once, wondrously, simply and yet manifoldly, itself a boundary to itself within itself, yet unbounded — by which it is, and is known to itself, and suffices to itself, unchangeably the same, through the overflowing greatness of its unity — who can readily grasp this? Who could express it in any way? Who would pronounce on it rashly, in any way?

Go on in your confession, say to the Lord your God, O my faith: Holy, Holy, Holy, O Lord my God, in your name we have been baptized, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; in your name we baptize, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because among us too, in his Christ, God made heaven and earth — namely, the spiritual and the carnal people of his Church. Yes, and our earth too, before it received the form of doctrine, was invisible and without form, and we were covered with the darkness of ignorance. For you chastened man for his wrongdoing, and your judgments were to him like the great deep. But because your Spirit was borne above the waters, your mercy did not abandon our misery, and you said, Let there be light: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Repent, let there be light. And because our soul was troubled within us, we remembered you, Lord, from the land of Jordan, and from that mountain equal to yourself, though made low for our sake: and our darkness displeased us, we turned to you, and there was light. And behold, we were once darkness, but now we are light in the Lord.

But as yet it is by faith and not by sight, for we are saved by hope; and hope that is seen is not hope. As yet deep calls to deep, but now in the voice of your waterspouts. As yet he who says, I could not speak to you as to spiritual people but as to carnal ones — even he does not yet think he has laid hold of it, and forgets what lies behind, and reaches forward to what lies ahead, and groans, weighed down, and his soul thirsts after the living God, as the deer after the water-brooks, and says, When shall I come? — desiring to be clothed with his dwelling that is from heaven, and calling down to this lower deep, saying: Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. And: Do not be children in understanding, but in evil be infants, so that in understanding you may be mature; and, foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you? But now no longer in his own voice, but in yours, who sent your Spirit from above, through him who ascended on high and threw open the floodgates of his gifts, so that the force of his streams might make glad the city of God. For him this friend of the Bridegroom sighs, though he already has the firstfruits of the Spirit stored up within him, yet still groans within himself, waiting for adoption — that is, the redemption of his body; for him he sighs, a member of the Bride; for him he is jealous, being a friend of the Bridegroom; for him he is jealous, not for himself — because it is in the voice of your waterspouts, not in his own voice, that he calls down to that other deep, over which, in his jealousy, he fears lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, their minds be corrupted away from the purity that is in our Bridegroom, your only Son. Oh, what a light of beauty that will be, when we shall see him as he is, and those tears will have passed away that have been my food day and night, while they say to me daily, Where is now your God?

Now I too say, O my God, Where are you? See — there you are! In you I breathe a little, when I pour out my soul on my own in a voice of joy and praise, the sound of one keeping festival. And yet again it turns sad, because it slips back and becomes a deep once more — or rather, it perceives that it still is a deep. To it speaks my faith, which you have kindled to light my feet in the night: Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord; his word is a lamp to your feet: hope and hold on, until the night — the mother of the wicked — until the wrath of the Lord has passed, the night whose children we too once were, who were once darkness, relics of which we still carry about in our body, dead because of sin — until the day breaks and the shadows flee. Hope in the Lord: in the morning I shall stand in your presence and gaze on you; I shall confess to you forever. In the morning I shall stand in your presence, and shall see the health of my countenance, my God, who will also give life to our mortal bodies through the Spirit who dwells in us — because in mercy he has been borne over our inner, darksome, drifting deep; from whom we have received, in this pilgrimage, a pledge that we should now be light, while we are saved by hope, and are children of light and children of the day, not children of the night, nor of the darkness, which we once were even so. Between them and us, in this uncertainty of human knowledge, you alone divide; you, who test our hearts, and call the light day, and the darkness night. For who discerns us, but you? And what do we have that we have not received from you? Out of the same lump, vessels are made for honor, just as others are made for dishonor.

Or who, but you, our God, made for us that firmament of authority over us in your divine Scripture? For it is said, Heaven will be folded up like a scroll; and now it is stretched out over us like a skin. For your divine Scripture holds a still more eminent authority, since the mortals through whom you gave it to us underwent mortality themselves. And you know, Lord, you know, how you clothed men with skins when by sin they became mortal. So too you have stretched out the firmament of your book like a skin — that is, your harmonizing words, which through the ministry of mortal men you have spread over us. For by their very death, that solid firmament of authority in the discourses they set forth was extended more eminently over all who live beneath it; while they lived here, it was not extended so eminently. You had not yet spread out the heaven like a skin; you had not yet enlarged in every direction the glory of their deaths.

Let us look, O Lord, upon the heavens, the work of your fingers; clear from our eyes that cloud which you have spread beneath them. There is your testimony, which gives wisdom to the little ones: perfect, O my God, your praise out of the mouths of babes and infants. For we know no other books that so destroy pride, that so destroy the enemy and the defender who resists your reconciliation by defending his own sins. I know no other words so pure, Lord, I know none, that so persuade me to confess, and make my neck supple to your yoke, and invite me to serve you for nothing. Let me understand them, good Father: grant me this, placed as I am beneath them — for it was for those placed beneath them that you established them.

There are other waters above this firmament, immortal, I believe, and separated from earthly corruption. Let them praise your name, let them praise you, the people above the heavens, your angels, who have no need to gaze up at this firmament, or to know your Word by reading. For they always behold your face, and there read, without any syllables in time, what your eternal will wills; they read, they choose, they love. They are always reading, and what they read never passes away; for by choosing and by loving they read the very unchangeableness of your counsel. Their book is never closed, nor their scroll rolled up, since you yourself are this to them, and are so eternally — because you have set them above this firmament, which you have firmly established over the weakness of the people below, where they might look up and learn your mercy, which announces in time you who made the times. For your mercy, Lord, is in the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds. The clouds pass away, but the heaven remains. The preachers of your word pass out of this life into another; but your Scripture is spread abroad over the peoples, even to the end of the world. Yet heaven and earth too shall pass away, but your words shall not pass away. For the scroll shall be rolled up, and the grass over which it was spread shall pass away with all its beauty; but your Word remains forever — which now appears to us under the dim image of the clouds, and through the glass of the heavens, not as it is: because even we, though we are already beloved by your Son, it has not yet appeared what we shall be. He looks through the lattice of our flesh, and he spoke to us tenderly, and set us aflame, and we ran after his fragrance. But when he appears, then we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. As he is, Lord, so will our sight be.

For, altogether as you are, you alone know — you who are unchangeably, and know unchangeably, and will unchangeably. And your Essence knows and wills unchangeably; and your Knowledge is and wills unchangeably; and your Will is and knows unchangeably. Nor does it seem right in your eyes that, as the unchangeable Light knows itself, so it should be known by the enlightened and changeable thing. Therefore my soul is like a land where there is no water, because just as it cannot enlighten itself, neither can it satisfy itself. For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light.

Who gathered the embittered together into one society? For they all have one end — a passing, earthly happiness — for the sake of which they do everything, though they toss up and down amid a countless variety of cares. Who, Lord, but you, said, Let the waters be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear, which thirsts after you? For the sea too is yours, and you made it, and your hands prepared the dry land. For it is not the bitterness of men's wills that is called sea, but the gathering together of the waters — for you restrain the wicked desires of men's souls and set them their bounds, how far they may be allowed to go, so that their waves break one against another; and so you make it a sea, by the order of your dominion over all things.

But the souls that thirst after you, and that stand visible before you (divided by other bounds from the society of the sea), you water with a sweet spring, so that the earth may bring forth its fruit, and, Lord God, at your command, our soul may put forth works of mercy each according to its kind — loving our neighbor by relieving his bodily needs, bearing seed in itself after its own likeness, when out of a feeling for our own weakness we have compassion enough to relieve the needy; helping them as we would want to be helped, were we in the same need — not only in the easy things, like the herb yielding seed, but also in offering the protection of our assistance with our best strength, like the tree yielding fruit: that is, doing good by rescuing one who suffers wrong from the hand of the powerful, and giving him the shelter of protection through the mighty strength of just judgment.

So, Lord, so, I beg you, let it spring up, as you do, as you give the cheerfulness and the strength: let truth spring out of the earth, and righteousness look down from heaven, and let there be lights in the firmament. Let us break our bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into our house. Let us clothe the naked, and not turn away from those of our own flesh. And when these fruits have sprung up out of the earth, see that it is good: and let our temporary light break forth, and let us, rising from this lower fruitfulness of action to the delight of contemplation, laying hold of the Word of Life above, appear like lights in the world, clinging to the firmament of your Scripture. For there you instruct us to divide between things of the intellect and things of the senses, as between day and night — or between souls given to things of the intellect and souls given to things of the senses — so that now it is not only you, in the secrecy of your judgment, as before the firmament was made, who divides the light from the darkness, but your spiritual children too, set and ranked in that same firmament (now that your grace has been laid open throughout the world), may give light upon the earth, and divide the day from the night, and be for signs of the times — that old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new; and that our salvation is nearer than when we first believed; and that the night is far gone and the day is at hand; and that you will crown your year with blessing, sending the laborers of your goodness into your harvest, in whose sowing others have already labored, and sending them also into another field whose harvest shall come at the end. Thus you grant the prayers of one who asks, and bless the years of the righteous; but you are the same, and in your years, which never fail, you are preparing a storehouse for our passing years. For by an eternal plan you bestow heavenly blessings on the earth in their proper seasons. For to one is given, by the Spirit, the word of wisdom, as it were the greater light; to another, the gift accompanied by the light of clear truth, as it were for the rule of the day. To another, by the same Spirit, the word of knowledge, as it were the lesser light; to another faith; to another the gift of healing; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discerning of spirits; to another different kinds of tongues. And all these are, as it were, stars. For it is one and the same Spirit who works all these, distributing to each person his own as he wills, and causing stars to appear plainly, for our benefit. But the word of knowledge, in which all the sacraments are contained — which vary with their seasons as the moon does — and those other, lesser tokens of gifts which are listed in order, as it were stars, since they fall short of that brightness of wisdom which gladdens the day already spoken of, belong only to the rule of the night. For they are necessary to such people as your wisest servant could not speak to as spiritual, but only as carnal — even he, who speaks wisdom among the mature. But let the merely natural man, still a babe in Christ and fed on milk, until he is strengthened for solid food and his eye is able to look upon the sun, not be left to dwell in a night forsaken of all light, but be content with the light of the moon and the stars. So you speak to us, our all-wise God, in your Book, your firmament, that we may discern all things in a wondrous contemplation, though as yet only in signs, and in seasons, and in days, and in years.

But first, wash yourselves, be clean; put away evil from your souls and from before my eyes, that the dry land may appear. Learn to do good, defend the cause of the fatherless, plead for the widow, that the earth may bring forth the green herb for food, and the tree bearing fruit; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord, that there may be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them shine upon the earth. That rich man asked the good Master what he should do to attain eternal life. Let the good Master tell him — the one he thought no more than a man, though he is good because he is God — let him tell him: if he wants to enter life, he must keep the commandments; let him put away from himself the bitterness of malice and wickedness — not kill, not commit adultery, not steal, not bear false witness — that the dry land may appear, and bring forth the honoring of father and mother, and the love of neighbor. All these, he says, I have kept. Where then do so many thorns come from, if the earth is fruitful? Go, root up the spreading thickets of covetousness; sell what you have, and be filled with fruit by giving to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and follow the Lord, if you want to be perfect, joined with those among whom he speaks wisdom, who knows what to give to the day and to the night — so that you too may know it, and lights may appear for you in the firmament of heaven; which will not happen unless your heart is there, nor will that happen unless your treasure is there too — as you have heard from the good Master. But that barren earth was grieved, and the thorns choked the word.

But you, chosen people, you weak things of the world, who have left everything to follow the Lord — go after him, and put the mighty to shame; go after him, you beautiful feet, and shine in the firmament, so that the heavens may declare his glory, dividing the light of the mature, though not as the angels, from the darkness of the little ones, though not despised. Shine over the earth, and let the day, lit by the sun, speak wisdom to day; and let night, shining with the moon, show knowledge to night. The moon and stars shine for the night, yet the night does not darken them, since they give it light in their measure. For behold, when God said, as it were, Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, there came suddenly a sound from heaven, like the rushing of a mighty wind, and there appeared tongues parting like fire, and it sat upon each of them. And there were made lights in the firmament of heaven, holding the word of life. Run to and fro everywhere, you holy fires, you beautiful fires; for you are the light of the world, and you are not put under a basket; he to whom you cling has been exalted, and has exalted you. Run to and fro, and be made known to all nations.

Let the sea also conceive and bring forth your works, and let the waters bring forth the moving creature that has life. For you, separating the precious from the worthless, are made the mouth of God, through whom he says, Let the waters bring forth — not the living creature that the earth brings forth, but the moving creature that has life, and the birds that fly above the earth. For your sacraments, O God, through the ministry of your holy ones, have moved amid the waves of the world's temptations, to consecrate the Gentiles to your name, in your baptism. And in the midst of these things, many great wonders were wrought, like great whales; and the voices of your messengers flew above the earth, under the open firmament of your Book — that firmament set over them as the authority beneath which they were to fly, wherever they went. For there is no speech or language where their voice is not heard, since their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world, because you, Lord, multiplied them by your blessing.

Am I speaking falsely, or am I mixing and blurring things together, failing to distinguish between the clear knowledge of these things in the firmament of heaven, and the material works in the surging sea and under the firmament of heaven? For of those things whose knowledge is fixed and unchanging, without any increase by begetting — the lights, as it were, of wisdom and knowledge — even of these, the material workings are many and varied; and one thing growing out of another, they are multiplied by your blessing, O God, who have relieved the weariness of mortal senses, so that one thing in the understanding of our mind may be expressed and set out in many ways by the motions of the body. These sacraments the waters have brought forth, but in your word. The needs of a people estranged from the eternity of your truth have brought them forth, but in your Gospel — because the waters themselves cast them out, the diseased bitterness of which was the reason they were sent forth in your Word.

Now all the things you have made are fair; but behold, you yourself, who made them all, are unspeakably fairer. Had Adam not fallen, the brackishness of the sea would never have flowed out of him — that is, the human race, so deeply curious, and swelling with storms, and tumbling restlessly up and down; and then there would have been no need for your dispensers to work, in a bodily and perceptible way, mysterious deeds and words amid many waters. For it is such things that these moving and flying creatures now seem to me to signify — through which people, once initiated and consecrated by bodily sacraments, would gain no further benefit unless their soul had a spiritual life, and unless, after the word of admission, it looked forward to what is complete.

And by this, in your Word, it is not the deep of the sea, but the earth separated from the bitterness of the waters, that brings forth — not the moving creature that has life, but the living soul. For it no longer needs baptism, as the pagans do, and as it itself once did when it was covered by the waters (for there is no other entrance into the kingdom of heaven, since you have appointed this as the entrance); nor does it look for the wonder of miracles in order to believe, for it is not such that unless it sees signs and wonders it will not believe, now that the faithful earth is separated from the waters that were bitter with unbelief; and tongues are a sign not to those who believe, but to those who do not believe. Nor then does that earth, which you have founded upon the waters, need that flying kind which the waters brought forth at your word. Send your word into it through your messengers — for though we speak of their working, it is you who work in them, so that they may produce a living soul in it. The earth brings it forth, because the earth is the cause that they achieve this in the soul, just as the sea was the cause that they worked upon the moving creatures that have life, and the birds that fly beneath the firmament of heaven, which the earth has no need of — although it feeds on that fish which was taken out of the deep, at that table which you have prepared in the presence of those who believe. For it was for this that he was taken out of the deep, that he might feed the dry land; and the bird, though bred in the sea, is nonetheless multiplied upon the earth. For man's unbelief was the reason for the first preachings of the evangelists; yet the faithful too are exhorted and blessed by them, in many ways, day after day. But the living soul takes its beginning from the earth, for it benefits only those already among the faithful to hold themselves back from the love of this world, so that their soul may live for you — the soul that was dead while it lived amid pleasures, death-bringing pleasures, Lord; for you, Lord, are the life-giving delight of the pure heart.

Now then let your ministers work upon the earth — not as upon the waters of unbelief, by preaching and speaking through miracles and sacraments and mysterious words, in which ignorance, the mother of astonishment, might be held intent upon them out of reverence for those hidden signs. For that is the way of entrance into the faith for the sons of Adam, forgetful of you, while they hide from your face and become a darksome deep. But let your ministers now work as on the dry land, separated from the whirlpools of the great deep: and let them be a pattern to the faithful, by living in front of them and stirring them up to imitation. For in this way people hear so as not only to hear, but also to act. Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live, that the earth may bring forth the living soul. Do not be conformed to the world. Hold yourselves back from it: the soul lives by avoiding what it dies by loving. Hold yourselves back from the unruly wildness of pride, the sluggish self-indulgence of luxury, and the false name of knowledge — so that the wild beasts may be tamed, the cattle broken to the yoke, and the serpents made harmless. For these are the movements of our mind, taken as an allegory: that is to say, the arrogance of pride, the pleasure of lust, and the poison of curiosity are the movements of a dead soul — for the soul does not die so as to lose all movement, but dies by forsaking the fountain of life, and so is taken up by this passing world, and conformed to it.

But your word, O God, is the fountain of eternal life, and does not pass away; and so this departure of the soul is restrained by your word, when it is said to us, Do not be conformed to this world — that so the earth may, in the fountain of life, bring forth a living soul: that is, a soul made self-controlled in your Word, through your evangelists, by following the followers of your Christ. For this is after its kind, because a person tends to imitate his friend. Be as I am, he says, for I too am as you are. So in this living soul there shall be good beasts, in the gentleness of action — for you have commanded, Go about your business gently, and so you will be loved by all — and good cattle, who neither overindulge if they eat, nor go without if they do not eat; and good serpents, not dangerous enough to do harm, but wise enough to be watchful, and inquiring into this temporal nature only so far as may be enough for eternity to be clearly seen, understood through the things that are made. For these creatures are obedient to reason when, restrained from prevailing over us to our death, they live, and are good.

For behold, O Lord our God, our Creator, when our affections have been restrained from the love of the world — by which we died through evil living — and have begun to be a living soul through good living; and your word, which you spoke through your apostle, is fulfilled in us: Do not be conformed to this world — there follows also what you immediately added, saying: But be transformed by the renewing of your mind; not now according to your kind, as though following a neighbor who went ahead of you, nor living after the example of some better man (for you did not say, Let man be made after his kind, but, Let us make man after our own image and likeness), so that we might test what your will is. For it was to this end that dispenser of yours spoke — the one who begot children through the Gospel — so that he would not have to keep them forever as infants, whom he must feed with milk and cherish like a nurse: Be transformed, he says, by the renewing of your mind, that you may test what is that good and acceptable and perfect will of God. That is why you do not say, Let man be made, but Let us make man. Nor did you say, according to his kind, but, after our image and likeness. For a man renewed in his mind, and beholding and understanding your truth, does not need another man to direct him so as to follow after his kind; but through your direction he tests what is that good, acceptable, and perfect will of yours; indeed, you teach him, now made capable, to discern the Trinity of the Unity, and the Unity of the Trinity. And so, to that which was said in the plural, Let us make man, is joined, in the singular, And God made man; and to that which was said in the plural, After our likeness, is joined, in the singular, After the image of God. In this way man is renewed in the knowledge of God, after the image of him who created him; and, having become spiritual, he judges all things — all things that are to be judged — yet is himself judged by no one.

But that he judges all things corresponds to his having dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and all cattle and wild beasts, and all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth. For he does this through the understanding of his mind, by which he perceives the things of the Spirit of God; whereas otherwise, man, though placed in honor, was without understanding, and is compared to the brute beasts, and has become like them. In your Church, therefore, our God, according to the grace you have bestowed upon it — for we are your workmanship, created for good works — not only those who are spiritually set over others, but those also who are spiritually subject to those set over them — for it was in this way that you made man male and female, in your spiritual grace, where, as far as the sex of the body goes, there is neither male nor female, because there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free. Spiritual persons — whether those set over, or those who obey — judge spiritually; not that spiritual knowledge which shines in the firmament, for they ought not to sit in judgment over so supreme an authority, nor may they judge your Book itself, even where something in it does not shine clearly — for we submit our understanding to it, and hold it certain that even what is closed to our sight is nonetheless rightly and truly spoken. For in this way man, though now spiritual and renewed in the knowledge of God after the image of him who created him, ought to be a doer of the law, not a judge of it. Nor does he judge that division between spiritual and carnal people, which is known to your eyes, our God, and which they have not yet revealed to us by their works, so that we might know them by their fruits — but you, Lord, already know them, and have divided and called them in secret, before the firmament was even made. Nor does he, though spiritual, judge the restless people of this world — for what business is it of his to judge those outside, not knowing which of them shall one day come into the sweetness of your grace, and which shall remain in the endless bitterness of ungodliness?

Man, then, whom you made after your own image, did not receive dominion over the lights of heaven, nor over that hidden heaven itself, nor over the day and the night, which you called into being before the foundation of the heaven, nor over the gathering together of the waters, which is the sea; but he received dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and over all cattle, and over all the earth, and over all creeping things that creep on the earth. For he judges and approves what he finds right, and disapproves what he finds wrong, whether in the celebration of those sacraments by which people are initiated, as your mercy seeks them out in many waters; or in that in which the Fish is set forth, which, taken out of the deep, the devout earth feeds upon; or in the expressions and signs of words, subject to the authority of your Book — signs that proceed out of the mouth and sound forth, flying, as it were, beneath the firmament, in interpreting, expounding, discoursing, disputing, consecrating, or praying to you, so that the people may answer, Amen. The speaking aloud of all these words is required by the deep of this world and the blindness of the flesh, which cannot see thoughts, so that there is need to speak aloud into the ears — so that, though flying birds are multiplied upon the earth, they still take their beginning from the waters. The spiritual man also judges, by allowing what is right and disallowing what he finds wrong, in the works and lives of the faithful: their almsgiving, as it were the earth bringing forth fruit; and the living soul, living by the taming of the passions, in chastity, in fasting, in holy meditation; and those things which are perceived by the senses of the body. Over all of these he is now said to judge, in which he also holds the power of correction.

But what is this, and what sort of mystery is it? Behold, you bless mankind, Lord, that they may increase and multiply and fill the earth — do you not thereby give us a hint, meant for us to understand something? Why did you not also bless the light, which you called day, nor the firmament of heaven, nor the lights, nor the stars, nor the earth, nor the sea? I might say that you, O God, who created us after your image — I might say that it was your good pleasure to grant this blessing to man alone — had you not, in the same way, blessed the fish and the whales, that they should increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea, and the birds be multiplied upon the earth. I might likewise say that this blessing belonged properly to creatures bred of their own kind, had I found it given also to the fruit trees, and the plants, and the beasts of the earth. But in fact it is said neither to the plants, nor the trees, nor the beasts, nor the serpents, Increase and multiply — even though all of these, like the fish, the birds, or men, do by generation increase and carry on their kind.

What then shall I say, O Truth, my Light? That it was said idly, and without meaning? Never, O Father of holiness — far be it from a minister of your word to say so. And if I do not understand what you mean by that phrase, let my betters — those with more understanding than I have — make better use of it, according to what you, my God, have given each person to understand. But let my confession too be pleasing in your eyes, in which I confess to you that I believe, Lord, that you did not speak so in vain; nor will I keep back what this lesson suggests to me. For it is true, and I see nothing to stop me from understanding the figurative sayings of your Bible in this way. For I know that a thing can be signified in many ways by physical expressions, though understood in one way by the mind; and that a thing understood in many ways by the mind may be signified in one way by a physical expression. Consider the single love of God and of our neighbor — by how many sacraments, and countless languages, and in each language by how many countless ways of speaking, it is expressed in bodily form. In this way the offspring of the waters increase and multiply. Notice again, whoever reads this: consider what Scripture delivers, and the voice pronounces in only one way — In the beginning God created heaven and earth — is it not understood in many ways, not through any deceptive error, but through various kinds of true meaning? In this way the offspring of man increase and multiply.

If then we consider the natures of the things themselves, not allegorically but literally, the phrase increase and multiply applies to everything that comes from seed. But if we take the words as spoken figuratively — which I rather suppose to be the intent of Scripture, since it surely would not attach this blessing, without purpose, only to the offspring of water creatures and of man — then we find that "multitude" belongs to creatures spiritual as well as bodily, as in heaven and earth; and to the righteous and the unrighteous, as in light and darkness; and to the holy writers who have served us as ministers of the Law, as in the firmament set between the waters and the waters; and to the society of people still caught in the bitterness of unbelief, as in the sea; and to the zeal of holy souls, as in the dry land; and to works of mercy belonging to this present life, as in the herbs bearing seed and the trees bearing fruit; and to spiritual gifts given for our building up, as in the lights of heaven; and to feelings shaped into self-control, as in the living soul. In all of these we meet with multitudes, abundance, and increase; but what increases and multiplies in the sense that one thing can be expressed in many ways and one expression understood in many ways, we find nowhere except in signs expressed in bodily form and in things conceived in the mind. By signs pronounced in bodily form we understand the generations of the waters, made necessary by the depth of the flesh; by things conceived in the mind, human generations, on account of the fruitfulness of reason. And it is to this end that we believe you, Lord, said to these kinds, Increase and multiply. For in this blessing I take you to have granted us a power and a capacity both to express in several ways what we understand as one thing, and to understand in several ways what we read as obscurely delivered in one. In this way the waters of the sea are filled, since they are stirred only by their many meanings; and in this way, by human increase, the earth too is filled, whose dryness shows in its longing, and over which reason rules.

I would also say, O Lord my God, what the Scripture that follows brings to my mind; yes, I will say it, and not be afraid. For I will speak the truth, with you yourself inspiring me to deliver what you willed out of those words. And it is by no inspiration but yours that I believe myself to speak truth, since you are the Truth, and every man a liar. He who speaks a lie speaks from what is his own; so that I may speak truth, I will speak from what is yours. Behold, you have given us for food every herb bearing seed that is upon all the earth, and every tree in which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed. And not to us alone, but also to all the birds of the air, and the beasts of the earth, and all creeping things — but to the fish and the great whales you have not given them. Now we said that by these fruits of the earth were signified, and figured in an allegory, the works of mercy that are provided out of the fruitful earth for the needs of this life. Such an earth was the devout Onesiphorus, to whose household you granted mercy, because he often refreshed your Paul, and was not ashamed of his chains. So too did the brothers who, coming from Macedonia, supplied what he lacked, bear such fruit. But how he grieved over certain trees that did not yield him the fruit owed to him, where he says: At my first defense no one stood by me, but everyone deserted me — may it not be held against them, I pray God. For these fruits are owed to those who minister spiritual doctrine to us out of their understanding of the divine mysteries — owed to them as men; and owed to them also as the living soul, which offers itself as an example in every kind of self-restraint; and owed to them also as flying creatures, for their blessings that are multiplied across the earth, because their sound went out into every land.

But it is those who are pleased by these fruits who are fed by them; those whose god is their belly take no pleasure in them. For the fruit is not found in the things given by those who give them, but in the mind with which they give them. He who served God, and not his own belly — I can see clearly why he rejoiced; I see it, and I rejoice with him. For he had received from the Philippians what they had sent him through Epaphroditus; and yet I can see why he rejoiced. For what he fed on was what he rejoiced over — for, speaking truthfully, he says, I rejoiced greatly in the Lord, that now at last your concern for me has flourished again, in which you were also concerned, but had no opportunity. These Philippians had, over a long weariness, dried up and withered, as it were, in bearing this fruit of a good work, and he rejoices for them, that they flourished again — not for himself, that they had supplied what he needed. And so he adds: not that I speak in respect of need, for I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content. I know both how to be brought low, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have been taught both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me.

What then do you rejoice over, great Paul? What do you rejoice over? What do you feed on, O man, renewed in the knowledge of God after the image of him who created you, you living soul of such great self-restraint, you tongue like the flying birds, speaking mysteries — for to such creatures this food is owed? What is it that feeds you? Joy. Let us hear what follows: notwithstanding, you have done well in that you shared in my affliction. This is what he rejoices in, this is what he feeds on: that they had done well — not that his distress had been eased, he who says to you, You enlarged me when I was in distress; for he knew both how to abound and how to suffer need, in you who strengthen him. For you Philippians also know, he says, that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving, but you alone. For even in Thessalonica you sent to my need, once and again. Over these good works he now rejoices, that they have returned; he is gladdened that they flourished again, as when a fruitful field turns green once more.

Was it for his own needs, because he said, You sent to my need? Did he rejoice for that? Truly not for that. But how do we know this? Because he himself says immediately after: not that I seek a gift, but I seek fruit. I have learned from you, my God, to distinguish between a gift and a fruit. A gift is the thing itself that is given, which supplies these necessities to us — money, food, drink, clothing, shelter, help; but the fruit is the good and right will of the giver. For the good Master did not only say, He who receives a prophet, but added, in the name of a prophet; nor did he only say, He who receives a righteous man, but added, in the name of a righteous man. So truly the one shall receive the reward of a prophet, the other the reward of a righteous man; nor does he only say, He who gives a cup of cold water to one of these little ones; but added, in the name of a disciple; and concludes, Truly I say to you, he shall not lose his reward. The gift is to receive a prophet, to receive a righteous man, to give a cup of cold water to a disciple; but the fruit is to do this in the name of a prophet, in the name of a righteous man, in the name of a disciple. With fruit was Elijah fed by the widow, who knew she was feeding a man of God, and therefore fed him; but by the raven he was fed only with a gift. Nor was the inner man of Elijah fed by that, but only the outer man, which might otherwise have perished for want of that food.

I will then say what is true in your sight, Lord: that when carnal men and unbelievers — for whose winning and initiation the initiatory sacraments and the mighty working of miracles are necessary, which we take to be signified by the name of fish and whales — undertake to give bodily refreshment, or otherwise help your servant with something useful for this present life, while remaining ignorant of why this should be done and to what end, then neither do they truly feed these, nor are these truly fed by them; because neither do the givers act out of a holy and right intention, nor do the receivers rejoice at their gifts, whose fruit they do not yet see. For the mind is fed by that in which it takes joy. And so the fish and the whales do not feed on such food as the earth does not bring forth until after it has been separated and divided from the bitterness of the waves of the sea.

And you, O God, saw everything that you had made, and behold, it was very good. Yes, we too see the same, and behold, all things are very good. Of each kind of your works, when you had said, Let them be, and they were, you saw that each one was good. Seven times I have counted it written that you saw that what you had made was good; and this is the eighth time, that you saw everything that you had made, and behold, it was not only good, but very good, now that it was all together. For taken one by one, they were only good; but taken altogether, they were both good and very good. All beautiful bodies show the same thing: a body made up of members that are each beautiful is far more beautiful than those same members would be by themselves, since by their well-ordered blending the whole is made perfect, even though each member on its own is also beautiful.

And I looked closely to find whether it was seven times or eight that you saw your works were good, when they pleased you; but in your seeing I found no times at all, by which I might understand how often you saw what you had made. And I said: Lord, is this not your Scripture true, since you are true, and being Truth, have set it forth? Why then do you tell me that in your seeing there are no times, when this very Scripture of yours tells me that what you made on each day, you saw that it was good — and when I counted them, I found how often. To this you answer me, for you are my God, and in a strong voice tell your servant in his inner ear, breaking through my deafness and crying out: O man, what my Scripture says, I say; yet Scripture speaks in time, while time has no bearing on my Word, because my Word exists in equal eternity with myself. So the things that you see through my Spirit, I see; just as what you speak by my Spirit, I speak. And so, when you see those things in time, I do not see them in time; just as when you speak them in time, I do not speak them in time.

And I heard, O Lord my God, and drank up a drop of sweetness from your truth, and understood that there are some who dislike your works, and say that you made many of them under compulsion of necessity — such as the structure of the heavens and the harmony of the stars — and that you did not make them out of what was your own, but that they were created elsewhere, out of other sources, for you to gather, compact, and combine, when, out of your conquered enemies, you raised up the walls of the universe, so that, bound down by that structure, they might not be able to rebel against you again. As for other things, they say you neither made them nor even put them together — all flesh, for instance, and all the tiniest creatures, and whatever has its root in the earth — but that a mind at enmity with you, and another nature not created by you and contrary to you, begot and shaped these things, here in the lower stages of the world. Those who say this are out of their minds, because they do not see your works through your Spirit, and do not recognize you in them.

But those who see these things through your Spirit — you see them in those people. Therefore, when they see that these things are good, you see that they are good; and whatever pleases them for your sake, you are pleased by it in them; and whatever, through your Spirit, pleases us, pleases you in us. For what man knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man that is within him? In the same way, no one knows the things of God, except the Spirit of God. Now we, he says, have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God, so that we might know the things that have been freely given to us by God. And I am reminded: truly, no one knows the things of God, except the Spirit of God — so how then do we too know the things given to us by God? The answer comes to me: because the things we know by his Spirit, these too no one knows but the Spirit of God. For just as it is rightly said to those who were to speak by the Spirit of God, It is not you who speak, so it is rightly said to those who know through the Spirit of God, It is not you who know. And no less rightly is it said to those who see through the Spirit of God, It is not you who see; so that whatever, through the Spirit of God, they see to be good, it is not they, but God, who sees that it is good. It is one thing, then, for a man to think that what is good is bad, as those mentioned above do; another thing for a man to see that what is good is good, as your creatures please many people because they are good, yet you are not pleased by them in those people, when they prefer to enjoy the creatures rather than you; and another thing still, when a man sees that a thing is good, for God to see in him that it is good — that is, that he himself should be loved in what he made, he who cannot be loved except through the Holy Spirit he has given. For the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who is given to us; and it is by him that we see that whatever exists, in whatever degree, is good. For it comes from him, who himself does not exist in some degree, but simply is what he is.

Thanks be to you, Lord. We behold heaven and earth — whether the bodily part, upper and lower, or the spiritual and bodily creation together — and in the adorning of these parts, out of which the whole fabric of the world, or rather the whole of creation, consists, we see light made, and divided from the darkness. We see the firmament of heaven — whether that primary body of the world, set between the spiritual waters above and the bodily waters below, or, since this too is called heaven, this space of air through which the birds of heaven wander, between those waters that are borne above it in vapor and, on clear nights, fall as dew, and those heavier waters that flow along the earth. We behold a surface of waters gathered together in the fields of the sea, and the dry land, both bare and, once formed, visible and well-ordered, along with the material of plants and trees. We behold the lights shining from above — the sun sufficient for the day, the moon and the stars to cheer the night — and that by all of these, times are marked out and signified. We behold on every side a moist element, filled with fish, beasts, and birds, since the thickness of the air, which carries the flight of birds, is thickened by the rising vapor of the waters. We behold the face of the earth adorned with earthly creatures, and man, created after your image and likeness, set, through that very image and likeness of yours — that is, the power of reason and understanding — over all creatures lacking reason. And just as in his soul there is one power that has dominion by directing, and another made subject so that it might obey, so too, in the body, was a woman made for the man, who in the mind of her rational understanding should have an equal nature, but in the sex of her body should in the same way be subject to the sex of her husband — just as the appetite for acting must draw the skill of right action from the reason of the mind. These things we behold, and they are, each on its own, good, and altogether very good.

Let your works praise you, that we may love you; and let us love you, that your works may praise you — works which have, in time, a beginning and an end, a rising and a setting, growth and decay, form and the loss of form. They have, then, their own succession of morning and evening, partly hidden, partly visible; for they were made by you out of nothing, not out of yourself — not out of any matter that was not yours, or that existed beforehand, but out of matter created at the same time (that is, created together by you) — because to its formless state you gave form, without any interval of time. For since the matter of heaven and earth is one thing and its form another, you made the matter out of sheer nothing, but the form of the world out of the formless matter — yet both together, so that the form followed the matter without any interval of delay.

We have also examined what you willed to be foreshadowed, whether by the act of creation or by the ordering of things in this sequence. And we have seen that things, taken singly, are good, and together very good, in your Word, in your Only-Begotten — both heaven and earth, the Head and the body of the Church — in your predestination before all times, without morning or evening. But when you began to carry out in time what had been predestined, so as to reveal hidden things and set right our disorders — for our sins hung over us, and we had sunk into the dark deep, and your good Spirit was borne over us, to help us in due season — you justified the ungodly, and divided them from the wicked; and you made the firmament of authority of your Book between those set above, who were to be teachable toward you, and those below, who were to be subject to them; and you gathered the society of unbelievers together into one conspiracy, so that the zeal of the faithful might appear, and they might bring forth works of mercy, even distributing their earthly riches to the poor, so as to gain heavenly riches. And after this you kindled certain lights in the firmament — your holy ones, holding the word of life, and shining with an eminent authority raised on high through spiritual gifts; and after that again, for the initiation of the unbelieving Gentiles, out of bodily matter you brought forth the sacraments, and visible miracles, and forms of words in keeping with the firmament of your Book, by which the faithful should be blessed and multiplied. Next you formed the living soul of the faithful, through feelings brought into order by the strength of self-control; and after that, the mind, subject to you alone and needing to imitate no human authority, you renewed after your image and likeness, and subjected its rational actions to the excellence of the understanding, as the woman to the man; and, for all the offices of your ministry needed to bring the faithful to completeness in this life, you willed that, for their temporal use, good things — fruitful for themselves in time to come — should be given by those same faithful. All these things we see, and they are very good, because you see them in us, you who have given us your Spirit, by which we might see them, and in them love you.

O Lord God, grant us peace — for you have given us all things — the peace of rest, the peace of the Sabbath, which has no evening. For this whole, most beautiful array of things very good, once it has run its course, is to pass away — for in them there was morning and evening.

But the seventh day has no evening, nor does it come to a close, because you have sanctified it to last forever — so that what you did after your works, which were very good, resting on the seventh day, even though you made them in unbroken rest, might, by the voice of your Book, announce to us beforehand that we too, after our works — which are very good, because you have given them to us — shall rest in you also, in the Sabbath of eternal life.

For then you will rest in us, as now you work in us; and so that will be your rest through us, just as these are your works through us. But you, Lord, are always working, and always at rest. You do not see in time, nor are you moved in time, nor do you rest in a time; and yet you make the things that are seen in time, and the very times themselves, and the rest that comes from time.

So we see these things that you made, because they exist; but they exist, because you see them. And we see outwardly that they exist, and inwardly that they are good; but you saw them there, when they were made, in the very place where you saw them still to be made. And we were moved to do good only at a later time, after our hearts had conceived through your Spirit; but before that, we were moved to do evil, forsaking you; while you, the one good God, never ceased doing good. And we too have some good works, by your gift, though not eternal ones; after them we trust to rest in your great sanctification. But you, being the Good that needs no good, are always at rest, because your rest is yourself. And what man can teach another man to understand this? Or what angel, another angel? Or what angel, a man? Let it be asked of you, sought in you, knocked for at your door; so, and only so, shall it be received, so shall it be found, so shall it be opened. Amen.
GRATIAS TIBI DOMINE
